newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Rwandan Hutus kill 63 in Burundi - state radio.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan Hutus kill 63 in Burundi - state radio.

text.p: Sixty-three people were killed when armed Rwandan Hutus attacked camps in Burundi's northwestern province of Cibitoke, state Burundi radio and army sources said on Monday.
Rwandan Hutu Interahamwe militiamen and troops from Rwanda's former army attacked two "regroupment camps" for Burundian peasants in Murwi and Buganda communes on Sunday, the radio said.
"They (Rwandans) attacked two regroupment camps and they killed 63 people and 12 have been wounded," the radio said.
Aid workers who travelled to Cibitoke on Monday reported seeing many bodies at Ndava commune, around 35 km north of the capital, apparently killed in the same incident.
"Our staff saw the bodies. Some were killed by bullet, some were lying there with severe wounds from axes, from machetes," said an aid worker, who declined to be identified.
"Apparently it was quite an indiscriminate killing. There were a lot of women and children (killed). In Ndava there were a large number of dead," an aid worker said.
One soldier died in the attack, and a total of 58 people were wounded, said army spokesman Major Mamert Sinarinzi, adding civilian casualties were taken to Cibitoke hospital.
Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army said last week it intercepted and killed 18 Rwandan guerrillas attempting to return to Rwanda from Zaire via Cibitoke. Burundi has close links to Rwanda.
Cibitoke lies between eastern Zaire and southwestern Rwanda. The Tutsi-dominated army in Rwanda is fighting an insurgency by former Hutu troops and militiamen, particularly in the west.
Regroupment camps were set up last year under military leader Pierre Buyoya, who seized power in a coup, to separate members of the ethnic Hutu majority from Hutu rebels battling the army.
Buyoya announced a pre-ceasefire agreement last week after direct talks in Rome with the main Hutu rebel group, the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
The province has been relatively quiet since Burundian Hutu rebels were driven from bases in eastern Zaire refugee camps last October, while the focus of fighting has shifted to the south and east.
More than 150,000 people have been killed in Burundi in massacres and civil war since 1993 when its first freely-elected Hutu president was killed in an attempted coup by Tutsi troops.
An estimated 800,000 Rwandan Tutsis and Hutu moderates were slaughtered in Rwanda in 1994 in a genocide by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs which fled when Tutsi rebels seized power the same year.

Rwanda and Burundi have the same ethnic makeup with a Tutsi minority and Hutu majority. Zairean rebels who seized the capital Kinshasa on Saturday uprooted Rwandan and Burundian Hutu rebels based in refugee camps in east Zaire late last year.
